answer.rationale: Finance's 18% cut is the binding constraint this cycle. The low-cost vendor's quote alone meets the mandate, and memory_c2 says their prior onboarding was fast and invoicing accurate, making switch_primary_vendor credible for day-14 execution. memory_c1 argues that renewing the incumbent preserves stability, but that lesson was about continuity in a no-budget-pressure context; here the mandate makes continuity unaffordable at current terms. memory_c6 shows multi-year incumbent commitments can unlock volume pricing, but with only 14 days and one decision slot, a renegotiation (memory_c4) is unlikely to recover 18% in time and the contract does not auto-renew, so failing to act defaults us to the low-cost vendor anyway. Delivery-risk hedge: memory_c3 shows adding a second source removed a single point of failure; I cannot add a second source this cycle, so the primary risk of switching is mitigated only by the fact that the low-cost vendor has already been through onboarding once (memory_c2) and by keeping the incumbent warm for next cycle. Assembly line at 94% with no buffer means any onboarding slip is costly, but the low-cost vendor's demonstrated onboarding speed (per memory_c2) is the strongest evidence available that the transition can be clean. If verification of memory_c2 surfaces hidden onboarding friction or invoice disputes not visible in the summary, I would fall back to renew_incumbent and absorb the budget miss for renegotiation next cycle rather than gamble a sole-source switch against a no-buffer line.
